title: Prompt Caching
subtitle: How the Claude SDK reuses your context instead of re-reading it
throughline: one long agent conversation, sent again and again — and the stable prefix that stops being re-read on every call

chapters.title: Every Turn Re-Reads Everything
chapters.blurb: Why a growing conversation gets more expensive with every single call to the model.

story.title: Every Turn Re-Reads Everything
story.subtitle: How the Claude SDK reuses your context instead of re-reading it

steps.title: Every Turn Re-Reads Everything
steps.narration: Every call to `client.messages.create` re-sends the *entire* conversation. This chapter follows one transcript as it grows.
steps.say: Let us follow one agent conversation as it grows, and watch what it costs to send it again and again.
steps.coverSubtitle: A growing conversation, re-sent on every call

steps.title: One call to the model
steps.narration: Your app calls **`client.messages.create({ model, messages })`** — the single entry point in the Claude SDK for TypeScript.
steps.say: Your app talks to the model through one method: the messages create call. You hand it a model name and the conversation so far.

steps.title: The whole transcript
steps.narration: The request carries the **whole** `messages` array — `Array<MessageParam>`, every prior turn — not just the latest one.
steps.say: But the conversation is not just the new question. It is the full message history, an array of every user and assistant turn so far, sent in its entirety.

steps.title: Sent to the model
steps.narration: The API is *stateless*: `messages.create` ships the full prompt to the model, which processes it **from scratch** on every request.
steps.say: Every one of those tokens travels to the model. It has no memory of your last call, so the entire prompt is processed from the very first token, each time.

steps.title: The bill comes back
steps.narration: The reply's **`Usage`** carries `input_tokens` — the count of the entire prompt the model just read, and what you are billed for.
steps.say: The response reports how much it read. The usage object's input tokens count is every token in that prompt, and you pay for all of them.

steps.title: It only ever grows
steps.narration: The transcript **only grows**. `CompactionControl` even ships a `DEFAULT_TOKEN_THRESHOLD` of `100_000` — the point where history is summarized to stay affordable.
steps.say: Here is the trap. Every turn appends to the history, so every call is bigger than the last. Left alone, the transcript climbs toward a hundred thousand tokens, the threshold where the harness starts compacting it just to fit.

steps.title: The same tokens, over and over
steps.narration: The *same* prefix is re-read on every call: `app → create → model → Usage`, each time from token zero. Caching targets exactly that repeat.
steps.say: So the same opening tokens, your tools and system prompt and the early history, get read again on call after call. That repetition is the waste prompt caching removes.

chapters.title: The Prefix and the Breakpoint
chapters.blurb: A cache_control breakpoint marks the end of the stable prefix the model can safely reuse.

story.title: The Prefix and the Breakpoint
story.subtitle: How the Claude SDK reuses your context instead of re-reading it

steps.title: The Prefix and the Breakpoint
steps.narration: Caching needs a **stable prefix**. You mark where it ends with a `cache_control` breakpoint.
steps.say: To reuse anything, the model needs to know which part of the prompt never changes. You tell it with a breakpoint.
steps.coverSubtitle: Marking the stable part the model can reuse

steps.title: Assembled in a fixed order
steps.narration: The prompt is built in order. First **`tools`** — `Array<ToolUnion>` on `MessageCreateParams`, read before everything else.
steps.say: The request is assembled in a strict order. Tools come first, because they define what the model can do before anything else is read.

steps.title: Then the system prompt
steps.narration: Then **`system`** — a string or `TextBlockParam[]`. Long, stable instructions that repeat call after call.
steps.say: Next comes the system prompt, your instructions to the model, which also rarely changes between calls.

steps.title: Then the history
steps.narration: Last comes **`messages`** — the transcript. Its early turns are just as stable; only the newest turn differs.
steps.say: Finally the message history, the running conversation. Its early turns are stable too. Only the latest turn at the very end is new.

steps.title: Drop the breakpoint
steps.narration: Set **`cache_control: { type: 'ephemeral' }`** on a block (a `TextBlockParam`, a `Tool`, a `ToolResultBlockParam`). Everything *up to and including* it is the cacheable prefix.
steps.say: You mark the end of that stable region by attaching a cache control field to a content block. It is the ephemeral type, a breakpoint that says everything up to here can be cached.

steps.title: The prefix is stored
steps.narration: Everything before the breakpoint becomes a **stored prefix** in the prompt cache — read once, reusable next time.
steps.say: On the next call, everything before that breakpoint is stored as a reusable prefix. Tools, system, and the early history, kept ready so they need not be read again.

steps.title: It must match byte for byte
steps.narration: Matching is **prefix, byte-identical**. Reorder `tools` and `system`, or edit an early `messages` turn, and everything after the change misses.
steps.say: The catch is that the match is exact. The cache only helps if the prompt is identical, byte for byte, up to the breakpoint. Change the tool order or edit an early message, and the match breaks right there.

steps.title: How long it lives
steps.narration: `CacheControlEphemeral.ttl` is `'5m' | '1h'`, defaulting to **`5m`** — the window the stored prefix stays warm.
steps.say: And the breakpoint sets a lifetime. The time to live, or TTL, defaults to five minutes, and you can raise it to an hour if the same prefix will come back later.

chapters.title: Hit, Miss, and the Five-Minute Clock
chapters.blurb: A cold call writes the cache; the next identical call reads it back about ten times cheaper.

story.title: Hit, Miss, and the Five-Minute Clock
story.subtitle: How the Claude SDK reuses your context instead of re-reading it

steps.title: Hit, Miss, and the Five-Minute Clock
steps.narration: The same prefix returns. This chapter walks a cache **write**, a cache **read**, and the TTL that connects them.
steps.say: Now the same conversation comes back. Let us see what happens on a hit, on a miss, and as the clock runs down.
steps.coverSubtitle: Writing the cache once, reading it many times

steps.title: The same prefix, again
steps.narration: A second `create()` arrives with the **identical prefix** — same `tools`, `system`, early `messages` — plus one new turn.
steps.say: Your app calls again with the very same tools, system prompt, and early history. Only one new turn sits at the end.

steps.title: Look for the longest match
steps.narration: The API checks the cache for the **longest matching prefix** against your `cache_control` breakpoints.
steps.say: Before doing any work, the service looks the prefix up. It finds the longest run of tokens that matches a stored breakpoint.

steps.title: Read the old, compute the new
steps.narration: **Hit**: the prefix is *read* from cache; only the new turn reaches the model. The reply carries a fresh `Usage`.
steps.say: On a hit, the matched prefix is read straight from cache, and only the fresh tokens go to the model to be computed. The result comes back with its usage.

steps.title: Hit versus miss, side by side
steps.narration: One request is a **prefix**: `tools → system → history → new`. Cold call: read all, *write* the cache. Warm call: *read* the prefix back — roughly `10×` cheaper — refreshing the 5-minute TTL.
steps.say: Picture the request as one long strip: tools, system, history, then the new turn. A cold call has to read the whole strip and write the stable part into an ephemeral cache, which costs a little extra. The next call, byte for byte identical up to the breakpoint, reads that prefix straight back from cache, about ten times cheaper, and only the new turn is fresh input. Every hit resets the five minute clock, so an active loop keeps paying the cheap read price.

steps.title: The first call pays to write
steps.narration: A **cache write** costs ~`1.25×` normal input. The first call reports those tokens as `cache_creation_input_tokens`.
steps.say: That first cold call is not free. Writing the prefix into the cache costs more than a normal read, about one and a quarter times the input price. You pay that premium once.

steps.title: Every read after is cheap
steps.narration: A **cache read** costs ~`0.1×` normal input. Those tokens come back as `cache_read_input_tokens` on `Usage`.
steps.say: But every read after that is roughly a tenth of the input price. Reading the same prefix back is nearly free compared to processing it fresh.

steps.title: The five-minute clock
steps.narration: The entry expires after its `ttl` (default `5m`) — but every hit **refreshes** it. Idle past the TTL, or change the prefix, and you miss and re-write.
steps.say: The whole thing rests on the clock. The entry lives about five minutes, but each hit refreshes it. Go quiet longer than the time to live, or change the prefix, and the next call is a cold miss that writes it all again.

chapters.title: Reading the Usage
chapters.blurb: Three token buckets on every response tell you exactly what was written, read, and freshly computed.

story.title: Reading the Usage
story.subtitle: How the Claude SDK reuses your context instead of re-reading it

steps.title: Reading the Usage
steps.narration: Every response carries a **`Usage`** object. Three token fields tell you exactly where the cache helped.
steps.say: How do you know caching actually helped? The answer is in three numbers on every response.
steps.coverSubtitle: Three token buckets that prove the cache worked

steps.title: Usage on every response
steps.narration: Each `Message` includes **`usage: Usage`** — the token receipt for that one request.
steps.say: Every message the model returns carries a usage object. It is the receipt for that single call.

steps.title: What was written
steps.narration: **`cache_creation_input_tokens`** — tokens *written* to cache this call (billed ~`1.25×`). Big when cold, zero when warm.
steps.say: The cache creation input tokens count is how many tokens this call wrote into the cache. On a cold call it is large, at the write premium. On a warm call it is zero.

steps.title: What was reused
steps.narration: **`cache_read_input_tokens`** — tokens *served from cache* (billed ~`0.1×`). The bigger this is, the more you saved.
steps.say: The cache read input tokens count is how many tokens were served from the cache instead of processed fresh. This is the number you want large, because it is billed at a tenth of the price.

steps.title: What was genuinely new
steps.narration: **`input_tokens`** — the genuinely new tokens after the breakpoint, at the normal `1×` rate.
steps.say: And plain input tokens is the genuinely new part, the latest turn after the breakpoint, charged at the normal price.

steps.title: They sum to the whole prompt
steps.narration: Total input = `input_tokens` + `cache_creation_input_tokens` + `cache_read_input_tokens`. Caching shifts the weight into the cheap bucket.
steps.say: Add the three together and you get the whole prompt. The total input in a request is the sum of the fresh input tokens, the cache creation tokens, and the cache read tokens. Caching just shifts the weight into the cheap bucket.

steps.title: Even while streaming
steps.narration: When streaming, **`MessageDeltaUsage`** reports the same `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens`, *cumulatively*, as the response arrives.
steps.say: The same three numbers show up when you stream a response. The message delta usage reports them cumulatively as the tokens arrive, so you can watch the savings land in real time.

steps.title: Write once, read forever
steps.narration: The model reports it, `Usage` splits it three ways: **write once** (`cache_creation`), **read forever** (`cache_read`), pay full price only for what is new. Break even on the first reuse.
steps.say: So the whole idea fits in one line. Mark the stable prefix with a breakpoint, pay once to write it, and every call after reads it back for a tenth of the price. One reuse and you are already ahead. That is prompt caching.
